description: Hi everyone! I'm a student/researcher interested in space exploration and game design. For this challenge, I'm planning to build a retro, pixel-art-style educational game where players manage a lunar outpost—balancing power, life support, and navigating hazardous terrain like permanently shadowed regions!
summary:
Lunar14 is an interactive game we developed to help children intuitively understand lunar missions during lunar daytime through hands-on trade-off experiences. Instead of simply selecting objects, players make decisions, manage power, and consider their physical condition, learning to allocate finite resources while navigating competing constraints.
Beyond gameplay, Lunar14 provides comprehensive post-game feedback, evaluating how players’ trade-off decisions affect future outcomes and whether they consider long-term consequences rather than immediate benefits. Even if players fail to complete the mission, they can restart from the exploration day where they believe they made an incorrect decision, allowing them to reconsider their choices and learn from their mistakes.
Each playthrough randomly selects one of the three most recent solar flare events recorded in NASA’s DONKI database, using its actual data to generate in-game events.
details:
What does it do, or how does it work?


Lunar14 is a browser game where kids aged 7-12 run a Moon base near the South Pole for seven days, with 24 working hours per day. One shared pool of power is split by five sliders that always add up to 100%: air, food, radiation shield, Earth communications, and science.

More for one means less for the others. Before sleeping, a Tomorrow Forecast simulates the next eight hours with the current settings.

On Day 5, a solar flare modeled on a real one strikes (X9.0, 3 Oct 2024; X8.7, 14 May 2024; or X9.3, 6 Sep 2017). Players have 25 seconds to pick a defense: an active shield (50 kW), a cabin barrier (3 hours), or nothing (risk to electronics).

They can also evacuate the astronaut during the last 3 game hours.

Benefits

  • Real trade-offs: every choice costs power, hours, food, or stamina; there is no free option.
  • Safe failure: a Commander explains each mistake, and players retry from their first mistake.
  • Open access: plays in any browser, with no account or download.
  • Traceable science: every fact shows its source in the game.

Intended impact


Instead of memorizing space facts, kids feel the tension of keeping a crew alive: the power bar drops, the flare alert flashes, and they have seconds to choose. They walk away with one lasting idea: in deep space, nothing is free, and mission planners decide using real data. Parents and teachers get an easy way to talk about solar storms, shielding, and astronaut health.

Next: live NASA DONKI data and a Mars outpost with communication delay.

Tools and technology

  • Architecture: runs from a single HTML file with no backend, so it loads quickly and is easy to deploy in any classroom.
  • Art and audio: all pixel art is drawn on an HTML5 Canvas (320x180), and all sound effects and music are generated with the Web Audio API, with no image or audio files.
  • Frontend: CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • Data: archived NASA SDO and NOAA GOES/SWPC flare records, NASA LRO Diviner, NASA/JPL, NOAA SWPC and NASA nutrition research, all labeled “archived, not live”.
  • Development: built with AI assistance (Claude), with automated browser tests.

How is it creative?
It turns an engineering idea into a slider a child can drag and instantly understand. The forecast teaches planning, not just reacting. Each playthrough uses a randomly chosen real flare, and its X number scales the damage.

What did we consider?

  • No free choice: meals, dust cleaning, shield boosts, evacuation, and repairs all have costs.
  • Accuracy: we verified numbers against NASA/NOAA sources and dropped claims we could not confirm.
  • Honesty: static data is never shown as live; simplified numbers are marked.
  • Ages 7-12: short sentences, a built-in glossary, taps to learn about buildings, and warnings in words, not only color.
  • Limits: the layout is not yet tuned for small phone screens, and the flare always arrives on Day 5.

In essence, Lunar14 turns real space weather into a decision children can feel: in space, nothing is free.
